utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, IT-95-14/2-T. The Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The diary. Yesterday afternoon it became clear, when the witness was spoken to on the narrow issue of the diary, there were some passages in the diary that he regards as personal, and that he didn't want poured over by others. I had to make a decision, given the order of the Court, that the witness shouldn't be spoken to about his evidence, as to the best way to get around the problem. And I hope the Court won't object that I suggested that, frankly, Mr. Kovacic speak directly to him about it. They speak the same language. And though I was present and there was an interpreter telling me roughly what was going on, I just let them get on with it. It seemed a sensible solution. I understand that there is now really no dispute, (a), as to the genuineness of the documents and the copies that we've got and, indeed, no dispute as to the fact that there are passages that are personal and that the witness would rather justifiably keep to himself. That, I think, leaves the position that what's extracted by us is not challenged as a genuine and proper extract. And I know that when Mr. Lopez-Terres selected the material he put in the summary, he selected on the basis that he thought the whole document would go in as a useful work of -- available reference, a useful part of the library to which we may all turn in due course if, as so frequently happens, something of detail becomes of value to one side or the other, in particular, matters of timing and things like that. So we would invite the Chamber to consider, in light of the new position, and the new information about the diary, the desirability of admitting it, because it may well solve problems later and save time generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is a vast amount of paper in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I understand that. And, of course -- I understand that. Some of that paper, for example, the ECMM reports that both sides produce and want to be produced, will serve as libraries, that is the same material to which reference may be made, but which doesn't have to be poured over by the Chamber or by those assisting the Chamber in the preparation of final documentation. But sometimes libraries are useful because they can suddenly become of value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll hear what the Defence have to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that yesterday's ruling stands and that we shouldn't be re-examining it. As for the issues raised in connection with that document, I would say the following: First of all, as my learned friend has said, the Defence is not disputing the authenticity of the copy. As the witness said towards the end of the hearing yesterday, we are not challenging that at all. We do indeed believe that the copies that have been produced are authentic copies of the original. A second point has to do with the wholeness of the document. We accept what the witness has said, that the sections which we have not seen refer exclusively to private matters. What is important here is that neither side, neither the Prosecution nor the Defence, has received those sections. Each side has the same document and the witness has just kept for himself, as he says, private notes that are in no way related to the extracts that we have received. The fourth point that has to be raised is the question of ownership of this document, because, after all, it is not quite clear whether this document, in view of the position he held at the time he wrote it, is it his property or the property of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be sensible to leave this ruling until we've heard the cross-examination, and then make a ruling on the document. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't have any position with respect to the diary. I wonder if, after the witness has testified, we could have a minute or two with the Court relating to the proposed testimony for the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly. Now, who is going to cross-examine first?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Cerkez defence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: NIHAD REBIHIC [Resumed]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Rebihic. As you heard yesterday, I represent the defence of Mr. Cerkez, together with my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic. I am an attorney from Rijeka. Should you fail to understand any part of my question, please ask me to repeat that question, without any hesitation. And please let us try and be as expeditious as possible so as not to waste time, and to bear in mind that what we are saying is being interpreted and, therefore, we should make breaks between the questions and answers. Fine. Tell me, please, at the beginning you informed us very briefly about your life and career prior to the conflict. May I just ask you, additionally, what you did between 1990, when you left MUP and retired, until 1992, when you joined the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I dedicated myself to my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in that period of time you had no position in any institution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you, during your testimony you said that, among other things, Sefkija Djidic said that Cerkez was one of the people who had probably distributed weapons from the SPS to the HVO, that is the Croats. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us refresh our memory. Is it true to say that towards the end of 1991 already, the JNA confiscated the weapons of the Territorial Defence and had it stored in barracks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The arms of Territorial Defence units, but the weapons of organisations of associated labour remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But the JNA tried to seize some of those weapons as well; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I was not active during that time, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the fact that certain decisions were taken by the management of the factory, I think these were related to decisions of the municipal authorities at the time, on the distribution of small arms to certain individuals in the factory and in the municipality, depending on the positions they held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, no, but I know later on when heavy weapons were being distributed, like anti-aircraft guns, I know that with relation to those, a decision was taken to share them half, half, between the TO and the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the weapons that were being used by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, I think you didn't keep your promise from the beginning, because this really is too fast for the interpretation, and it is difficult to follow. So will you please slow down a little bit. I think it's easier to follow the content if you go more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, Your Honours. My fault.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So what you just said, heavy weapons in the possession of the factory for its own protection in the event of war were distributed by agreement between the TO and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that such an agreement was reached, but how it actually was distributed, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But then you learnt that some small arms were also distributed, if I understood you well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that Cerkez was the assistant in Stjepan Tomasevic and that later he became brigade commander; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know when, exactly, Cerkez became commander of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, I was in Visoko, so I can't tell you exactly. I was at the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But do you know roughly when this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you do not know that the Vitez Brigade --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness's stated knowledge, really, at this point, doesn't seem to be very relevant. As far as the Trial Chamber is concerned, we'll have evidence as to when Mr. Cerkez took over. And Mr. Kovacic, with respect, there is no need to go through this with every witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You devoted a considerable amount of the time during your testimony yesterday to incidents that occurred in Vitez and the surroundings, or rather in the municipality. Can we agree that in fact the majority of those incidents occurred between autumn '92 and the beginning of 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were the most turbulent times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Would you agree that the incidents were provoked by both sides?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You claim that all incidents in that period were provoked by the Croats and HVO members, and that there wasn't a single incident provoked by members of the BH army or any individuals, independent individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say that there wasn't a single incident, but the vast majority of incidents was provoked by the conduct of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In this Trial Chamber, through some other witnesses, we have seen reports by Ivan Budimir. Do you recall? As an intelligence officer, you must have been aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, at the time, I was not an intelligence officer. I acquired that role in May 1993. At the time, I was deputy commander of a voluntary detachment participating in the battle front in Visoko. Afterwards I was a co-ordinator of those units, and later on assistant commander for training, so I was not an intelligence officer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Rebihic, but during this period, end of '92 and beginning of 1993, you were in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, for instance, the event of the 20th of November '92, when certain members of the BH army seriously wounded six members of the HVO military police and two civilians, confiscated their weapons, and among those BH army members was somebody called Edin Livnjak, known as Dino? This was a story that was widespread at the time. Do you remember that event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do remember some story to that effect. Whether I was in Vitez at the time, or Bijelo Bucje, or in Visoko, I don't know, but I did hear about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the incident of the 13th of January, 1993, in Vitez, when again, members of the army captured and disarmed eight HVO members, and then that there were negotiations between Sefkija Dzidic and Pasko Ljubicic about the restoration of their weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If my memory is correct, this must have been in the territory of Zabilje. This was in response to a previous incident, when, again, I can't remember the exact number of members of the BH army went to take over their shift in Bijelo Bucje, and they were not allowed to pass, and they were disarmed and their weapons confiscated. And then came the reaction, and I think that that was when those home-made explosive devices were found on them, if that is what we are talking about, known as MRUD.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You use the word "reaction." Weren't all incidents a kind of action and reaction, a cause-and-effect relationship between them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot allege that, because a very large number of incidents were directed against innocent civilians without any cause.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, for instance, the 17th of January, 93, in Sadovace, when again a group of members of the BH army captured seven HVO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is precisely what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is the town 110?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the 17th of January, in Kruscice, when members of the army disarmed 17 HVO members coming from the front, near Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Apropos, do you remember -- and this was outside Vitez municipality -- that on several occasions members of the HVO who were going to the front line against the Serbs near Turbe were stopped, searched, identified, and so on, and there was a lot of talk about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me not list all the other incidents. You agree, therefore, that there were incidents on both sides, but mainly that the blame lay with the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a local, you could distinguish between local people and others, and in connection with those incidents yesterday, you mentioned members of the Ludvig Pavlovic Brigade, whom you had referred to as Herzegovinians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't know what their exact name was, but these were people from Herzegovina. They could be recognised by their dialect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: From your testimony yesterday, it follows that they caused quite a lot of disturbance in town; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the Vitezovi also provoked unrest in the town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that the situation in the town and the surroundings was rather disorderly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean, "disorderly"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean there was a lot of uncertainty, frequent infractions of the peace.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that all this was provoked intentionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Regarding the Herzegovinians, I found a note in your diary which I think refers to the 12th of January, 1993, when you explicitly mention the presence of HVO units from Herzegovina in Vitez, and their temporary accommodation, after which they would be sent to the battle front in the region of Mt. Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we had information to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And finally, they did leave Vitez, but they never went to Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not to Vlasic, but they left Vitez. It is a fact that some of them were seen later on. Some may have left, but some did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Witness, in the course of 1992, in Vitez municipality, a crisis staff of the municipality was formed with representatives of both peoples and people appointed ex officio?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were you ever invited to attend meetings of that institution in connection with assignments that it issued or reports that needed to be given on events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So, personally, you were never invited?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the main aim of that Crisis Staff was to try and maintain peace in Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, throughout we sought to keep the peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The politicians on both sides and as well as representatives of the armed forces of both sides, that is the TO and the army and the HVO and the other, participated in those endeavours to keep the peace and to maintain balanced relationships?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, talks were held regularly, but the conclusions of those talks were not implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Among other incidents, you mentioned one, which I thought was particularly unfortunate. You said that some HVO soldiers had entered a school, a classroom, and forced Muslim children to remain standing for 50 minutes. Do you have any knowledge as to who those people were, which soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We received that report from the parents of those children, and after that Muslim children no longer went to school. They stopped going to school. And I do not know who they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that this occurred at the end of January 1993, did anyone on your side try to investigate this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not within my mandate to investigate those things, and I am not aware whether anyone else did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In your diary there is an entry for the 20th of August 1992. I would call it an incident. And you noted that a certain Medugorac from Cajdras with another four persons demolished facilities in town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, trying to establish what this is about, I found that this Medugorac was a member of the HOS, as far as I know. Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: His name could have been Jako. Are you quite sure that his name was Goran?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure. Those were reports that were available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Perhaps this might refresh your memory. Jako Medugorac, who was registered as a member of HOS, was taken into custody a little later in Kaonik because of a crime he had committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You hadn't heard that the Croatian military police or, rather, the HVO military police had arrested him there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I only heard about Miroslav Bralo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday about the line-up of the HVO in Vitez in the summer of 1992. Let us clear that up a little. The parade was held in August 1992; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was in Visoko, so I didn't watch the parade, but only later, from the media, from the local television, I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, you know that before this parade, a couple of months before that there was a similar ceremony of the Territorial Defence forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, outside the secondary school centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So both sides would invite representatives of the other side to those ceremonies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was customary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Both those ceremonies were not held in any kind of secrecy; on the contrary, they were televised? Please say "yes" for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were not there and that you just saw a report on television about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you claim that you saw Cerkez delivering a speech on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you see him surveying the units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not personally. On television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the voice of the commentator that we heard on the video, was that the voice of Anto Marijanovic? Yesterday we could see clearly that Anto Marijanovic was making the speech.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So he was the one speaking at the parade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, before the official touring of the units. Then first came the speech and then the review of the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the commentator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that anyone else made a speech? Did you see anyone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that on local television I saw the speech, I saw Cerkez in person. I didn't see Marijanovic, because I just happened to look when this was being broadcast. So I didn't watch the whole event.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time, so we are talking about the summer of 1992, the aggression of the JNA against Bosnia was fierce; it was under way at the time? There is no doubt about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And that is why I placed my services at the disposal of the staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did both these parades symbolise preparations of both Muslims and Croats for the struggle against a common enemy and for the defence of their territories?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what it appeared to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it a fact that within this small territory of your municipality and the surrounding municipalities, the TO, which has grown into the army and the HVO, jointly held the front towards the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot be certain about that. In the case of Vitez, I cannot know for other areas. But I am -- I was a participant, together with other TO members, by then army members, and we regularly held the front line at Visoko and the area of Bijelo Buce, and on one occasion just above Turbe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So these areas just above Turbe, you will agree that the HVO from Vitez also held a part of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I was probably in Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But, for instance, in March and April, in February 1993, at the beginning of 1993, while you were still there, the HVO kept a part of the front line at Strikanac, Lopar with at least two platoons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of that. I know that the HVO was located with its artillery in the area of Mescema, in the second line its task being to provide support, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were in Bijelo Buce, above Goles. This position was trigometric point 60. I don't know the trigometric point, the grid reference number. Ibrahim Puric was the commander there, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the Vitez unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, but I am talking about your unit at that position.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. His name was Puric, but his first name was not Ibrahim. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So on the flank of that line, wasn't there Kamenjas, Lopar, a sector which was held by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that belongs to the Novi Travnik area. Kamenjas does belong there. I heard of that position, but I can't give you any details because I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were in Bijelo Buce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but only when I went to review the positions. I said that I was the co-ordinator of the units, and as the co-ordinator I was in charge of the timely shift changes and the full -- and keeping the manpower at its full strength. And so I only came to the Bijelo Buce when I would come into the village to the school building in order to ascertain what was needed for the troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Kovacic, you've asked a great deal about this. Do you want to pursue the matter? In which case, I shall ask a question. Or we must move onto another topic. Mr. Rebihic, were there HVO troops on the front line or not? Could you just answer that, whether there were or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, it seems little point going on with this. If you want to call other evidence about it, you are welcome to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one follow-up question regarding the ceremony and the parade. From what we could glean on the TV report, there were a number of women wearing camouflage uniforms. I believe there were even some camouflage skirts. Was this a usual thing at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did see several young women in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would that necessarily mean that they were members of the army or would that have been some kind of a trend or even fashion, to just don parts of the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I really cannot comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So after the parade, at that time in Vitez there was a Territorial Defence staff and also, with respect to the HVO, that is its military side, there was the HVO headquarters. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the HVO headquarters was the branch, so-to-speak, of the HVO authority in Vitez, which was in charge of the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, basically these were volunteers who would go on the shift and carry out their tasks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that Marijan Skopljak was chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, Marijan Skopljak held a position in the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean in 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about later on. I know that he was in that position, but I don't know if he was then replaced by someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in your understanding, in 1992 he was a municipal chief of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is how I -- that is what I knew about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You also gave evidence that on the 19th October 1992, in the evening hours, you saw a massing of the HVO troops in front of the hotel, and in that area of Vitez, that is where the police station was and the gas station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19 October. What I was referring to was the gathering of members at -- at midday. I don't know if that's what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. You said that you saw a large number of vehicles, a lot of HVO soldiers, and among other vehicles there was a Raba and then a truck and then there was an anti-aircraft gun and -- is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. But that happened during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So it was during the day. You later stated that you received reports that in Novi Travnik only 27 HVO members from Vitez were registered; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We received that in a fax transmission from the HVO -- from the headquarters in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: If that was the size of the force -- in other words, only 27 members -- where did the balance of the force go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But 27 is a number which is less than what you had assessed previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, don't argue, please, with the witness. He said he doesn't know. Now, if a witness says he doesn't know, there is no point pursuing it. You can make your own comments in due course when you come to address the Court; you can call witnesses. But let us move on, rather than trying to argue with the witnesses to get them to agree to your point of view, which they may well be unwilling to do. So now let's go on from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, if that was the impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me refer you to your diary. In it, in the entry of 31 October, which is twelve days later, you refer to the list of the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I said that we received a fax transmission from the TO headquarters with that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll ask you several questions regarding this list. First of all, did you have any knowledge that at least a majority of the names on that list were of HOS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not research the list, I just noted down as it came, because it was not my task to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that at the same time, the HVO units from the surrounding municipalities, including Vitez, did send significant forces to fight in the defence of Jajce against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us move on. You mentioned a meeting held in the night between the 19th and 20th of October 1992. You said that at that time a man was already killed at the barricade in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, this was a man called Salkic, or perhaps Pezer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Didn't you, then, maybe enter the time of the meeting in error? Because the purpose of the meeting and the other two meetings which took place on that day and that evening when the barricade was erected, the purpose was to find a solution; that is, before the incident at the barricade took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The incident at the barricade did occur on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't recall when the meetings took place a day before that confrontation at the barricade? Or was it not then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The meeting you are referring to was after the incident, and its purpose was to try to calm down the situation and to overcome the misunderstandings and to avoid the conflict. That was the purpose of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Regardless of potential errors or mistakes regarding the date, do you recall that on the eve of the conflict at the barricade, there were also several meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But not at the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at the headquarters, but members of the headquarters participated at it. Mr. Dzidic was there, politicians were there, solutions were being sought, there was an attempt made to overcome the problem? Just say "I know," "I don't know," "I remember," or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only recall the meeting the next day at the post office, where the UNPROFOR representatives mediated, as well as other European officials, with the aim to calm down the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You spoke about the attack against the TO, and you mentioned the Dzidic/Cerkez conversation over the phone, and you claimed that Cerkez said that it was Darko Kraljevic's Vitezovi who was attacking the TO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was talking on the phone with Dzidic, and when Dzidic was telling Cerkez about the situation that was going on around the TO, I clearly heard Cerkez saying that it wasn't his units but Darko's units that were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And that information was further corroborated through other sources?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never did corroborate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you agree that these were not those troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see them, and I didn't know. Then we were transferred, we moved to Stari Vitez, and I never followed it up in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you were not trying to find out what unit forced the headquarters to relocate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and it was not my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now that we've touched on the HOS and Darko Kraljevic, throughout this period, he had an independent force in Vitez and the surroundings, especially in certain parts of that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if he was independent, but I only know that he commanded these troops in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean Kraljevic did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Kraljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the areas where they were present, more or less, would they include Kolonija, Rijeka? That is, the southern part of Kruscica, around the forestry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that is where he lived. That is where his home was. That is where they gathered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, he was at the school in Dubravica. That was noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the killing of two ABiH soldiers at the Kruscica road near Pero Skopljak's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not Pero Skopljak's house; Marijan Skopljak's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: My apologies. You're absolutely right. It was Marijan Skopljak's house. You said that those people were killed by some Croats. So these were not members of the HVO units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I clearly stated that those members of the army were in some coffee bar, and they found there several armed members of -- I don't know what unit, but they were Croatian soldiers who left before the ABiH army left, and set up an ambush, and these two members of the ABiH were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that mixed or joint investigative teams were set up to investigate these crimes, and they didn't come up with anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they were mixed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they produced no results?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you said that in respect of this specific incident, nothing happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not aware of this case ever being solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me read to you what Mr. Ramo Vatres says of this on the 24th of September, '97.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, there's no point trying to get this witness to comment on what somebody else may have said somewhere. I don't know, Mr. Kovacic, what you were going to read from, but there's little point in that. He said that he wasn't aware of the case being solved, and that's as far as you can take it with him. Now, it may be that there is some other evidence that you can call upon the subject, in which case, do so. But again, there is little point arguing with a witness who says he doesn't know. Can we move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I accept this. I would just like the Chamber to know that we have no proof, but we received this statement from the Prosecution. It was given by a witness who apparently was not going to be called, and this is the only opportunity I have to put it to the witness and see if he has any recollection about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can attempt to put it in; it may be that it's something which the Prosecution will agree. But you can put the matter in whatever way that you choose in due course. Do you know anything more about this particular case, Mr. Rebihic, than what you've already told us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing else. This is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's move on. You mentioned that the only case that you were aware of where criminal proceedings were instituted against someone, an individual called Bralo, or Cicko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you say, on the basis of any fact, that he was a member either of the Stjepan Tomasevic or Viteska brigades at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know a member of which unit he may have been, but through a conversation with a soldier who was detained -- actually captured by the TO headquarters. In fact, he came to the front line on his own will, and perhaps not knowing that that is where the front lines were, so he just showed up there. So in talking to him, I learned that when he spoke -- that he had heard of Bralo when Vladimir Santic referred to him and said, "Now that Cicko has arrived, you'll see how things are getting done."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on. You mentioned the presence of the Tigers or Tigrovi of General Praljak, and this was a delegation which included Arif Pasalic, Jasmin Jaganjac, Anto Prkacin, the only Croatian general in the BH army, and they came to discuss the joint command and the strengthening of the joint defence against the JNA aggression?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You were notified in advance that these meetings at the highest level were to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the Tigers to whom you referred were the escort of this delegation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the information received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Rebihic, we will agree that they just passed through Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know nothing other than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you see them in Vitez at any time later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Later on, there was a reference made about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't know who the source was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we are at it, wasn't there talk about this joint command which was to be established, that it should include Merdan from the BiH side, and Nakic from the HVO side, who would be the point persons in this joint command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And they started operating and their headquarters was in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next incident when you were arrested when driving in a vehicle. You were going to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On this road between Vitez and Travnik, at that time which is immediately preceding the conflict, how many checkpoints were there which one had to clear to when moving from Vitez to Travnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started from Stari Vitez towards Travnik, and the official checkpoint was at the intersection of Novi Travnik and Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And who held that checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who held.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know who held it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that it was Croatian troops, but the soldier who made me step out of the car --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, we'll get to that point. But do you know at least whether that was a military checkpoint or a police checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know that they had camouflage uniforms on. I don't know whether they were police or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There were no other checkpoints on that stretch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No checkpoints controlled by the BiH side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were arrested and taken to Dolac, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Dolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Dolac, the place where you were arrested, is within Travnik municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested at the crossroads and driven to Dolac, where there was also a unit of the HVO. Again I saw HVO members in uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But Dolac is outside Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dolac does not belong to Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Finally, you told us, after the mistreatment and your release, the vehicle, you learnt, was retained by Darko Kraljevic. Did you ask him to give it back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I never had any contact with him. This was what I was told at the checkpoint, at the crossroads. I know that the commander, Sefkija, intervened with Cerkez to ask for the vehicle to be returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But relations between Sefkija and Cerkez were correct, were they not, throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When anything needed to be done quickly, the two of them understood one another and spoke quite frankly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were acquaintances and they got on quite well. I can't get into any details, but I think they did cooperate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: One further point. Those who arrested you, were they the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know whether they were the military police. I was quite shocked at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any visible insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. At the checkpoint there were people with the military police insignia on their left sleeves. Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned, on the 14th of April, a group of Muslims from Vitez going to work in Bratsvo in Novi Travnik were also arrested. They were arrested in the territory of Novi Travnik municipality; were they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit arrested them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also mentioned that the anniversary was being observed of the formation of BiH, and you said that Cerkez came as a guest and that you yourself spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rebihic, some of the activities connected to the celebration were held during the 14th and the 15th, over two days in other words. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Cerkez was in the premises of the municipal TO staff in connection with that celebration on the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the day you met him was the 15th, and you are quite sure it was the 15th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unless I've become senile. But, you know, it's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then on the 15th in the evening you saw again concentrations of various HVO units in Vitez, in the evening. You saw that yourself, or did you receive reports to that effect, or was it a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally could not have seen it, because I wasn't in town and I didn't say I saw it. We were informed by telephone, by citizens from town. And this was also confirmed by an officer of the British Battalion, Captain Matthews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it means you learnt about the concentration of troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was present when this officer was conveying this report to Commander Sefkija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A little earlier on, let us go back to the 3rd of March, I think it was, when you said that the Croats had hoisted their flag in the SPS. Talking about the flag, do you remember that at the beginning of April, during celebrations of Bajram in 1993, a large flag was hoisted in Vitez near Vitcom across the whole road which you had to pass going to Stari Vitez, and that it was therefore a long time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it was not at Vitcom. The flag was hoisted in the immediate vicinity of the mosque. Vitcom is too far away for the flag to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. But we are talking about the same road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But it was a large one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Like transparency. Don't you remember that there was some dissatisfaction over this flag? And anyway, whose flag was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you see, we in the staff sought at all cost to avoid provoking any potential reaction, and in the course of the Bajram festivities it is customary, it is a religious flag of the faithful that we had hoisted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It stood there for some time, and none of the Croats made a fuss about it, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true, that it stood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This flag in the SPS did cause a lot of concern among certain currents on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This flag was hoisted in an organisation of associated labour, at the entrance, at the gate leading to the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that on the first day of the conflict, with a hand-held transmitter, which you called a walkie-talkie, you were intercepting HVO radio communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any more sophisticated equipment for interception of radio communications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our equipment was extremely modest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you only used this hand-held transmitter/receiver for interception, nothing more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us exactly what kind of radio transmitter it was, its brand, its type?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you the brand. We received those radio transmitters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] -- what the brand was. Can we not move on? This sort of detail doesn't assist the Trial Chamber. Now, Mr. Kovacic, is there any dispute about this particular conversation? There is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may just briefly -- one statement, sir. [Interpretation] We believe that technically it was impossible for him to intercept, but I will ask the witness. The statements referred to are misinterpreted, but I wanted first to show that this was not possible. And I must try to prove that, otherwise I will have to bring expert witnesses who will be able to testify as to radio stations and their capacities. My plan is to show him pictures of some radio transmitters used by the HVO, to recognise them and to tell us whether they had such equipment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Rebihic, do you know what sort of a radio it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can describe it very well. I don't know the brand, because we received them, I think it was on the 7th of April from our workers from Switzerland. I personally went to Rijeka to pick up the equipment and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There has to be a limit to the amount of evidence we can have on one particular issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we are through with his radio station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, you can put to the witness these pictures, but do it quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I ask the usher for his assistance, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rebihic, you will now be shown several pages of photographs, so will you please look through them and tell us whether you can identify any of that equipment as being in the possession of the HVO in Vitez or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think there is no need for me to look, because I didn't see the HVO radios.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the issue is not what the HVO had. The issue is what he heard. Now, look, if you would, at these documents which are being produced. They are not very good photocopies, anyway. Just have a look, Mr. Rebihic, and see if you can identify any of these or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is similar to this radio station. I can't say that that is it. I know it had three buttons, one for channels, one for volume, and that is it, for sound adjustment. But I don't know any further detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Yes. Let's go onto the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you claim that listening to communications among HVO members you were able to recognise the voice in this case of Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not something I claim. It is something I am absolutely certain of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, how did the participants identify themselves?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, allow me to say. You are aware of our position regarding equality of arms. You cannot, in a cross-examination, nevertheless, spend 20 minutes on the same issue. We know what a cross-examination is. You keep asking the same question to the witness. Please, try and do your work within the framework of a cross-examination, which is simply a verification of the examination-in-chief. Now, this becomes really excessive. This is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him certainly how he recognised Mr. Cerkez's voice. If you want to do that, of course you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you recognise Mr. Cerkez's voice by the colour of the voice or the way in which he spoke and how he punctuated his words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Cerkez extremely well, because we communicated, we conversed. I know by his way of speech, by the sound, by the tone of his voice, that it was Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the participants in these communications identify themselves with numbers or did they use pseudonyms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They communicated with numbers, unit reports to number 3, 23 reports to number so and so. But in that conversation I clearly recognised the participants, Cerkez and Marko Lujic. I know them very well and I'm absolutely certain that I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you heard Cerkez's conversation on two occasions only?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And on that second occasion, it was a conversation with Marko Lujic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you gave us your interpretation, but let me read what is written in your diary. This says, "1317 hours: Mario, can you hit what you hit a moment ago" -- that above the "K," that is "J," in brackets, Jelovac -- "and do it well." From this note of yours, it follows that the voice that you recorded here, that this person is addressing somebody called Mario rather than Mario being the one who is speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. As soon as I heard the voice, I wrote immediately the name "Mario," because I recognised him. And then the text is quoted verbatim, what he said. "Jelovac," in brackets, is what I wrote, because I followed the previous fire, and it was directed in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But there is no colon after the word "Mario," and there are no quotation marks, but you will agree, this was wartime; what did the other person say, then, at the other end of the line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably nothing, and that is why I didn't note anything down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, what is most important of all, regardless, whoever gave that order, this "J" that you interpreted as being "Jelovac," what kind of a target is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is an elevation point. That was probably an orientation for the targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it's not a house, or a village, or a hospital, or any other unacceptable target?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. That is just the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you perhaps show us on a map where Jelovac is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think that we had a very good map from the previous witness, Z2175. It's a very good copy, 2175.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We haven't any exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't see this very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps you could help him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please look, and then, when you find it, show it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it's here. Krcevine, Gradac, I think it's here. This one here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is elevation point 629?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Witness, will you tell me, please, whether you know that the mentioned Marko Lujic, the person you mention in this conversation, has a son in the HVO whose name is Mario?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you didn't know that, thank you. Very well. Let's go on to the next topic. You spoke about the truck bomb, the fuel truck that exploded in Stari Vitez. You mentioned that you saw two fuel trucks before, parked not far from the house of Mario Skopljak. Could you please, Witness, tell me whether you recall that a company had already been formed under the name of Vitez Trade, owned by Marijan Skopljak, Markesa, and some other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I saw those fuel trucks near the house of Mario Cerkez, and not Mario Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well then, let me ask you in greater detail. The distance between Cerkez and Mario Skopljak, what is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not very far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So those fuel trucks were on a piece of socially owned land which was suitable for parking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you haven't answered my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About Vitkom [sic], I know that it is operating now, but as for those days, I wasn't aware of that, nor did it interest me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean Vitez Trade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Vitez Trade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to assist us and to give us excerpts Z2210,9, these birth certificates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're referring to the death certificates?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Could the witness look at those documents, please, to leaf through them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Do I need to identify them?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, I just have one question about them. Look, please, at all four documents. In the top, you will see a different time indicated as the time of death, registration of the time of death, the line just below the heading. This line here [indicates]. Will you look at the first line below the letters in bold print?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see. It says, "18th of April, 1993"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No, not that, above that, when it says the certificates, the death certificates and the number, 93, 95, 94, 95. These data are not related to the date of death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But allow me to put my question to you. You were a member, you were an officer of MUP, you were aware of the procedure. How can we see that these deaths were registered subsequently? There must be a legal basis for such a registration, subsequent registration. You worked on these things in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there must be a reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The only legal grounds, unless there is a death certificate, is a procedure declaring a person who is missing as being dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but those bodies were not operating at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was the procedure then, and even today, and it was the responsibility of the court, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see what's the point of discussing that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We have both been asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is true that it is clearly regulated, but there wasn't a joint registrar operating at the time, and these are abstracts from the book of death certificates issued subsequently, probably at the request of relatives, and you have to register the year when the death was recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the bottom of the document we have the date of issue of the document; that is fine. But in all four of these documents, it is noted that the registration was done on the basis of a decision by the police. For some a date is indicated; for others there is no date. Can you explain why the police --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Before you do, is there, Mr. Kovacic, any dispute that these people were killed in the explosion caused by the truck bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are sure that people were killed on that occasion, but we don't know whether there is any reliable data to indicate who. But these documents seem to indicate that it was these particular people who were killed, so I'm actually challenging the formal regularity of these documents. That is all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, well, we've got that point. Now shall we move on to another one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us about the exchange procedure and your activities in the Exchange Commission. You first said, in that connection, something that I am interested in, that Cerkez misled you because he said that he had no prisoners, and upon your arrival at the cinema hall you found that there were 13 prisoners there, or detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said, and that is correct and true. That can be verified at the UNPROFOR camp, where there is a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rehibic, you know that those persons -- because you discussed that matter that morning -- that those 13 people were brought there maybe a half hour or an hour previously from Kaonik to the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Talking to those people, they told us that they had spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Some of them testified here, and their testimony differed from that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember very well the conversations we had in the cinema hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Those persons were brought from Kaonik by the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But from your general knowledge, did you know that Kaonik was under the control of the military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All I know about Kaonik was that it was a prison. Who controlled it, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that in the course of that conversation, Cerkez told you that he considered those people to be safer in detention than at liberty. Do you believe that he was implying that he was holding them there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I clearly heard Cerkez say that he believed that they were safer there than they would be in their own apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this corresponded to the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot confirm or deny that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. As regards the families that you mentioned and the dispute over whether they could leave town, the family members were not detained at the time, were they? It was just a question of whether they would be allowed to leave the town and pass through checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to be able to leave with their husbands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, it's now 11.00. Would that be a convenient moment to adjourn?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Half an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And to conclude about the visit to the cinema theatre in respect of the release of prisoners. At that time, those present included the representatives of the HVO civilian government, Messrs. Ivica Santic and Mario Skopljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not about the release.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they talk with people in that regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And just the last question in that regard. Who, eventually, approved the -- who approved that the families of these people could leave Vitez, that is, people who opted to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That was after the conversation which you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Regarding the exchange commission of which you were a member, which you mentioned, Z903 was offered here. That was the joint command of Messrs. Kelestura and Cerkez on the establishment of this commission. Kelestura and Cerkez issued this order and it -- as ordered to do so by a superior command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is not in dispute that Kelestura and Cerkez signed this order pursuant to an order which directed them to do so signed by Petkovic and Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they were tasked as local commanders to implement the agreements reached at a higher level; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were one of the persons who received certain specific tasks as a member of the commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So your membership of the municipal staff of the Territorial Defence was not of importance here; you were just delegated to get the job done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. With your permission, Your Honours, I can clarify this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The joint commission was established by the HVO and ABiH representatives, and Refik Hajdarevic was delegated by the ABiH army. He was from the 325th brigade, and myself as member of the TO headquarters. And Mr. Borislav Jozic and Stipo Krizanac were delegated on the part of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday you mentioned at least on two occasions some shelling on the first day of the conflict. At one point you stated that you could, by the sound of these grenades, you said that you were able to ascertain the 150 millimetre calibre, also nicknamed as Nora, was used on Preocica, and you said that you were in Stari Vitez and that you could see this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Visually speaking, I could not see the position from which the fire was -- that the weapon was fired, but I know that it was from the Mosunj area. But you could see the impact, that is the explosion in the area of Preocica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you conclude this on the basis of your own perception?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you have seen Mosunj from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that visually I could not see it, but I could hear it. So acoustically, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the same way you concluded or you inferred that artillery fire was used from Mosunj in the direction of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Again, the weapon was fired in the area of Mosunj, and the impact was heard in the direction of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll change the topic. But let me just ask, since you had the military education. What is the range of such a gun? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My knowledge of this matter was from the 70's. I wasn't actively involved in the military affairs, but based on the sound and the explosion, this must have been a larger -- a higher calibre weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's now focus on some events in Mahala itself. You said that your headquarters was there and that you also kept a military unit there. There was also some equipment and some weapons, were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the unit is concerned, at that time it was not deployed there because the attack prevented this, so the units of 325th brigade or the municipal headquarters were never established there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. According to the information we have, and Mr. Sefkija also testified in another case on this, as far as Stari Vitez is concerned there was one 82 millimetre mortar in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see it. I am -- I know of two 60 millimetre mortars being present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At least three snipers --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am only aware of one, and I don't know if you are referring to the 7.9 millimetre rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was one of them a Steyer 7.9 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Believe it or not, I never saw one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Our information is that there were at least six M-52 machine guns, also 7.9 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then there was one M-84 machine gun and in stock there were at least ten rocket --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go into any details about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And there were a lot of small arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as the small arms is concerned, it was used by the military police, the civilian police, and some local inhabitants who were members of the units which we have mentioned and who happened to be in Vitez at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that 30 military police soldiers were armed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that -- again the same number, but there were 30 members of the civilian police under arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I guess these numbers can be established. I wasn't there, and I told you about the establishment of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And some 210 other armed people, so that all in all there were about 270 armed men in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe that that is -- that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In the end, the fact is that Mahala managed to survive until the final peace was signed, and it never fell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When we spoke about the attack of the 17th July, you said that one of the killed was named Zlatko Nakic, and you said that he was a member of the military police, which was part of the Viteska Brigade. Do you know that the 4th battalion of the military police was deployed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO military police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know Mr. Zlatko Nakic personally. He was part of the escort of the mixed commission of which I was a member, and the military police of the army and the HVO were in charge of providing escort, so I don't know whether that has anything to do with the 4th Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question in another way: Is it true that the military police had its headquarters in the Hotel Vitez, that is, the HVO military police, or the 4th Battalion of the HVO military police? Just say if you know or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In that respect, I can only say that I had heard of some regional military police whose command was on the upper floors of the civilian police, in the former premises of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You also mentioned that a soldier was killed, and you identified him -- that is, killed on the HVO side -- whose identification showed that he was a member of ZNG, Zenga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It was the home guards? "ZNG" stands for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You're not aware of the fact that this formation was disbanded as early as 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you are not saying that a unit from Croatia was involved in the attack against Mahala?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just said that on the basis of this identity card, this is what I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Later on, you mentioned some other topics, and if I can quote you, at one point you said that in the zone of responsibility, any zone of responsibility, the commander of the largest unit is responsible for the entire area of responsibility; did I quote you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in Vitez, the Central Bosnia Operative Zone command was superior to him? That is, individually speaking, General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I know the hierarchy, the commander of an Operative Zone is superior to all units in that zone. And at the local level, and that is how I framed my statement, the commander of the largest unit in that area is in command of that zone of responsibility and is superior to all other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in the area of Vitez, in those days when the conflict broke out, what was the zone of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that Vitez was in the area of responsibility of the Viteska Brigade. I don't know farther afield.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
