utterances.text: But is it true that some other HVO units were also active in Vitez and operating in Vitez, in that area? And some of them you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because evidence shows so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. On your side -- that is, the ABiH side -- did the 325th Mountain Brigade have its own zone of responsibility, or was it responsible for the entire Vitez municipality area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a member of the Territorial Defence staff. The zone of responsibility of that staff was Old Vitez. As far as deployment of the brigades outside of this territory, I could not know much from Stari Vitez, so I cannot really give you a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday we had Exhibit Z1009-1 introduced. Can I please have it shown to the witness? With the Court's permission, we received this supporting material, an almost identical document, and it was dated 10 June, '93. We never received the original; we only received a translation of it. May it be distributed to all the parties, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let that be distributed, if you have it. Mr. Kovacic, are you coming to an end of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, Your Honour, I think that that is the last question I have -- I mean, a couple of questions connected to the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Rebihic, you have a document before you which we saw yesterday. The version you have in front of you is in the language you understand. We have a translation of this document, and to your right, on the ELMO, is a copy of the document which is a translation of the document. We never received the original; we only have this translation. If you look at the document to your right, which is in English, you will see that there is a name starting each paragraph, and at the bottom it states that it was signed by you as the deputy commander, and there is an abbreviation which I believe refers to your position as an intelligence officer. Can you tell me, in addition to the documents of 2 June, 1993, you also drafted a similar document, an almost identical document, of 10 June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is no dispute that I signed these documents at the request of the superior bodies of the army, and the documents state clearly that it refers to the relevant intelligence information I received at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In both of these documents, about 20 persons were named, and from the heading, it would follow that these 20 persons were those whom you suspected were responsible for committing crimes or directly connected to the crimes and genocide against the Muslims in the area of Vitez municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not how I understand this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we read -- why don't you read the title?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It says that there is grounds or reasons for -- reasonable grounds to suspect, so it doesn't say that they were responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Rebihic. Could you say, out of the persons named in these two documents, some of them are the persons whom you reasonably suspected of having committed crimes, and Mario Cerkez is not among them? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it was stated in one of these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. Rebihic, if you can just answer the question. This is a simple question. Perhaps the Prosecutor can follow up with his own questions, but a total of 14 names mentioned in these two reports, some of them are repeated in both, but I just want you to answer whether the name of Mario Cerkez is among these individuals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what to tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, the answer is no, it's not. Now, can we next move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, did you at any time, and even following the Dayton Agreements, you shared this information with the Croatian side, that is with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I left the army immediately following the Washington agreements and dedicated myself to the family, and I have no further knowledge of what transpired subsequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would conclude my cross-examination. And I thank you, Mr. Rebihic. Your Honour, I would like that this document, the second one dated June 10, would be entered as the evidence in the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number will be D40/2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Naumovski. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the defence of Mr. Kordic has no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few questions, a few points of clarification for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: It was indicated during your testimony by the defence that you had dealings with a certain person called Budimir. Could you tell us who Mr. Budimir was? I think his name is Ivan Budimir. In a few words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Ivan Budimir was a teacher. I know him personally. I know that for a time he was commander of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was Mario Cerkez his superior in the chain of command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Logically, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You spoke about the military police of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. It was also specified, during the cross-examination regarding the events of the 20th of November 1992, you were asked whether you remember an incident concerning the arrest of six members of the Croatian military police and the injuries inflicted on two Croatian civilians. Do you recall that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Today?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Yes, today, by the representative of the defence. He mentioned an incident when Croats were wounded by members of the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said that I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: That incident, according to what was said, occurred on the 20th of November 1992, but we agree that the death of two soldiers named Huso Kargic and Sead Hurem occurred in the night, between the 19th and 20th of November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: An observation concerning a date referred to by the defence. They referred to an incident concerning people in Cajdras as if it occurred on the 20th of August 1992. I think that was a mistake, because the diaries that we have attributed to the month of October 1992, and not August. As regards the 3rd of March 1993, we spoke about it yesterday, and you noted in your diary that on that day a Croatian flag was hoisted in front of the SPS factory. And this morning reference was made to the hoisting of a flag which you described as a religious one near the mosque during the celebrations of Bajram?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Will you agree with me in saying that the day when the Croatian flag was hoisted in front of the factory, not only was the flag hoisted, but all the guards of the factory were disarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Therefore, the problem was not merely a problem regarding the flag?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Before that the security officers were disarmed and removed from their working places.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Regarding the work of the commission in which you participated, the commission formed on the 11th of May 1993, and the founding document being signed by the accused, Mario Cerkez, and Mr. Mensud Kelestura. This is Exhibit Z903. On this document in paragraph 3 the following is indicated: "Each party should provide a vehicle for the military police, as well as a vehicle for the needs of the commission."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And, if I understood you well, it was on that basis that Zlatko Nakic was a member of the military police -- that you learnt that he was a member of the military police during work in that commission?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This document was signed by the commander of the Vitez Brigade and the commander of the 325th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The two parties, therefore, are the Vitez Brigade and the 325th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Still in connection with this commission, you drafted a report which was previously admitted as Z2712, a report on the 24th of May 1993. In that report you mentioned the 15th of May 1993, that the commission dealt with various matters, and in the afternoon the commission visited the cinema and was able to talk to people who were arrested and detained in the cinema?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So that was the 15th of May as the date of that visit. The defence noted a moment ago, in the course of the cross, that the witness who testified here had said that they were released the same day from Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In my conversation with the people, in the presence of others, and there were representatives of the HVO in attendance, the prisoners clearly said that they had spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let me specify for the attention of the Trial Chamber the two witnesses who have already testified, Witness J, and another witness, Mr. Edib Zlotrg, indicated when they testified in this Chamber that it was on the 14th of May that they were released from Kaonik and not on the 15th of May. Therefore, there must be a mistake made by the defence a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, can we speed up? We've got another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am also done.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You indicated, in connection with the speech made by Mr. Cerkez during this parade at the Vitez stadium, you said this morning that the ceremony was organised to struggle against a common enemy, which were the Serbs at the time. Yesterday, in the speech that you referred to, there was reference to the arming of Croats against the Muslims, and not against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I clearly said yesterday, and today as well in the course of my testimony, that every effort was made to avoid a conflict in Vitez. In this speech that I referred to yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Rebihic, simply, did Mario Cerkez in the speech he made indicate that the Croats were threatened and that they have to protect themselves from the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Regarding the 19th of October 1992, when you saw the concentration of forces in the centre of Vitez, you never said that these were exclusively forces that were stationed in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: There may have been among them forces coming from outside Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Regarding the presence of soldiers that you described as Tigrovi, Tigers, who escorted General Praljak. In the period we are referring to, General Praljak was the head of the HVO, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what his position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: He was a Croatian general from the Republic of Croatia, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know that from talks I had that he was a Croatian general, but what position he held, I don't know. And that he came with the aim of establishing a joint command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You didn't know that General Praljak had a position of authority within the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Finally, regarding the reports that were shown to you this morning with lists of names, the reports that you signed as an assistant commander of the intelligence service. What was the exact purpose of those reports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the burial of the bodies, from superior army authorities the headquarters was required to provide a report on information in its possession regarding events that had occurred within the territory of the municipality. The aim was to inform higher level competent bodies of the information at the disposal of the municipal TO staff at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Those reports were not intended to list all the names suspected -- of people suspected of committing crimes in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. The information that we had at that time, until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with my questions to the witness. I have a request on behalf of the office of the Prosecution regarding the diaries that we discussed at length this morning. The Office of the Prosecutor believes, after close study of those diaries, that it would be necessary for the Chamber to directly familiarise themselves with those diaries, and that they should be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, do you still maintain your objection to the introduction of this diary?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I understood that it is solved, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's out, but they're asking it to be in. Let's deal with the witness first before we go on with this. Mr. Rebihic, I'm sorry to have kept you. Your evidence is now over. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thought that you had made your ruling yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been asked to reconsider it. We wanted to know whether you maintained your objection or not. Yes or no will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We maintain our objection. We were just trying to contribute practically and to be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It remains out. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness is Mr. Allan Laustsen. We've received an offer of proof last night, and I don't want to take up too much time, but it seems to the Kordic defence, from looking over this, that this testimony is completely duplicative of the testimony already given by Major Baggesen, who unfortunately was detained before the Trial Chamber for quite a few days. The second problem is that it also deals with the issue of the Zenica shelling on April the 19th, and the Trial Chamber has already heard about that from Major Baggesen. The third point that we would make concerns very specifically paragraph 9. Apparently Mr. Laustsen is a Danish police inspector who was also an ECMM monitor, and with all due respect to the witness, it seems to us that the opinions that he wants to give in paragraph 9 surely fall beyond the competence of a police officer, and so we would object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to deal with this for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, in fact, it's Mr. Scott who's dealing with this witness, and I'm just arranging for him to come in. I think the general reply is that this witness is in any event going to be dealt with quite swiftly; I think Mr. Scott's forecast is of about 45 minutes in chief. In any event, the proper time to deal with these objections is really item by item, when we see what, if any, validity there is in the objections. The summary doesn't necessarily set out the full experience and relevance of what the witness is able to say. It looks, from Ms. Verhaag's solitary return, as though neither the witness nor Mr. Scott is in the right place at the right time, for which I apologise, but I would respectfully invite the Chamber simply to deal with this on an item-by-item basis if and when we reach the problem areas, because I know, in relation to matters of expertise, that this witness probably holds rather than is shown in the bare outline, but I'll ask Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, it may well be that matters about Zenica have been disputed, and therefore he is certainly entitled to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But how much of the other is going to assist us and isn't simply repetitive of what Mr. Baggesen said is something which we ought to look at rather carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Scott will have that in mind in any event, he having called Mr. Baggesen himself, and he knows which matters would be duplicative. I think that's the reason he thinks that the evidence will be so short in any event. While he's -- sorry, perhaps I shouldn't cut across your line of thinking, because he's got to arrive, and he hasn't yet arrived. It's clear we're going to finish the witness one way or another today; there is no tightness of timetable now. There are a couple of administrative matters that I would like to touch on, and may I just use a couple of minutes now to deal with one of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's the recurring issue of the mapped front lines that the Chamber has sought. Providing it has been, obviously, a fairly extensive exercise, because it means drawing on material from different places, and then, having got the material together, the question of how it's going to be presented that's in a way most useful to the Chamber and probably in a way that's most portable to the Chamber, because where you can have big visual aids in a courtroom like this, if you can't take them away with you to work on, they're probably less valuable than more. Having looked at various versions that are already in the form of preparation, I have provisionally come to the view that you might actually be assisted more than anything else by something very simple, namely by the map that I know some members of the Chamber have been referring to, the coloured map -- I don't know what the exhibit number is -- suitably overdrawn in different versions with the front lines at different dates, so that you have two or three more copies of this map, and at this scale. There's always a problem of what scale of map to have. If you have it too big, the thing ceases to be portable. If you have it too small, you can't read a thing. Now, if this map, folded as it has to be, is broadly a useful tool to the Chamber, and if the Chamber are happy with that, I'll try and have it printed, or rather overprinted, with the front lines at different dates, and then there will be a similar map specific to Vitez. If that doesn't seem a very helpful suggestion, and if the -- it's not for me to ask questions, I know, but if the Chamber has any alternative proposals for how it would like the material presented, then I'll see if I can meet the request. But sometimes all modern sophistication can't beat something fairly traditional; namely, a map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, it sounds a sensible suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll have that commissioned. I was told yesterday that the prospects are that the printing can be done by the end of next week, but I'll get it to you as soon as possible. What I would propose -- I hope this won't cause any disquiet -- I propose to put the map in as a tool at this stage. We'll have to get a witness to come along and derive its markings in due course; that may be an additional witness, or it may be one of the existing identified witnesses providing this material, but it may be a useful working document, subject to proof. I wasn't padding out time, but I notice that Mr. Scott arrives just as I finish dealing with that small matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There is no dispute on anything; I just want to be useful, let's say. In the Blaskic case, there was a three-dimensional model used, and I'm not talking about the value as evidence on that material, but it is obviously something which everybody could easily see the situation and everything. Perhaps we can think about the use of that material and have it in the courtroom so it's easy to show what is where, and perhaps some marks on the front could be added.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I've already dealt with that model. A, it only shows part of the area; and B, for a reason that was wholly unexplained, it's completely out of scale, so that it doesn't give anything like an accurate picture of the terrain, making it look more like a ski resort than the place that it is. It's also heavily overmarked with alleged identification of forces of one kind or another, which by no means is necessarily agreed, and it would not, in our respectful submission, be of any value in this case, dealing with a much wider area and where precision is required. Can I just explain privately the position to Mr. Scott so that he can know what's afoot?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, I think that Mr. Nice has explained to you the situation. We think that it was you, in fact, who examined in chief Witness Baggesen, and we believe that much of the summary that you have presented is repetitious of what has already been said, with the exception of the two or three last pages. So we would like to ask you to focus on the substance and not to repeat what we already know, and which has already been stated here, and that is one of the principles of procedure that we wish to pursue more and more, and that is not to admit repetitious testimony by this Tribunal, in the interest of efficiency and justice. So will you please bear that in mind so that we can finish with the witness, including the cross-examination, before the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you. I think by the technique of leading, by skipping certain material and leading on other material, I predict, Your Honour, that this can be -- the entire direct examination can be quite brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, is it correct that you are a career officer in the Danish police?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your present rank is chief inspector?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You became an ECMM monitor assigned to RC Zenica as of approximately 1 April 1993, and left the region on approximately the 1st of July 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The head of RC Zenica during your duty was Jean-Pierre Thebault?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that when you began your duties with ECMM you were briefed, and one of the items covered in your briefing was the ECMM assessment that the senior political leader in Central Bosnia was Dario Kordic who, perhaps among other things, was identified as the vice-president of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that during the month of April 1993, you were teamed with fellow monitor Lars Baggesen in team Z1, and after that you worked again with both Mr. Baggesen and another monitor named Bent -- I think it's pronounced Faerge?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your areas of responsibility included Zenica, Kakanj, Breza, Visoko, Kiseljak, Fojnica, and Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you were the operations officer, in fact, at RC Zenica for approximately the month of June 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that it was the general perception or position of ECMM, RC Zenica, during the time period from April through June, that is your tour of duty, 1993, that the HVO was attempting to take full control of the proposed Vance-Owen provinces 8 and 10, even though there were Muslim majorities in wide areas?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you ever hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, if you are doing paragraph 9, it's subject to dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I was going to try to approach it slightly differently, if I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In connection with your testimony just now about Vance-Owen provinces 8 and 10, did you ever hear what was presented as the Bosnian-Croat plan presented using any particular terminology about a particular territory or a particular state?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I do object to that. This involves a pure political opinion from this witness, and I don't mean any disrespect to the witness, but I really do question how helpful that's going to be to the Trial Chamber. Obviously, that's for the Trial Chamber itself to decide, but a pure political opinion from essentially a lay witness is --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me respond to that, please. If I can respond briefly, please. This is not a personal opinion from just this witness. This was the informed assessment of the ECMM which was these were professional people, sent there as trained observers by the European community for the exact purpose of analysing and coming to certain -- making observations and coming to certain conclusions. This was -- I believe the witness -- he didn't think of this on his own. This was the ECMM assessment at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Scott, I think that you may have other witnesses, people responsible in the ECMM to ask them for their conclusions. You do not necessarily need to ask this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that can be said about a number of things. The answer would have been answered -- quite frankly, the question would have been answered by now. A number of people, you are right, could address this, but I see no reason why this witness shouldn't be able to give his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, we don't think it's going to assist. If you'd move on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that around Easter of 1993 you learned that there had been trouble in the Travnik area, when the HVO raised a Croatian flag there which resulted in a confrontation in which two ABiH soldiers were shot and killed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it also reported around that time that the HVO was taking up military positions on the high ground around Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: To your knowledge, sir, is it correct that HVO checkpoints on both sides of Travnik, we are now talking about around the Easter period of 1993, began stopping all vehicles on the road, and it was reported that many Muslim civilians were arrested at these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You recall, sir, and is it correct that on the 12th of April 1993, a convoy of approximately four trucks containing wheat flour were hijacked in the Vitez area by the HVO at an HVO checkpoint?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you learn, and not only you, but RC Zenica, learn around the 16th of April 1993 that indeed there was heavy fighting in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your own investigation, sir, is it correct that you determined that the HVO headquarters in Vitez was not in fact attacked on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: When I visited the place, there were no signs of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. In the interest of speed, I may have skipped a point. Did you learn and was RC Zenica informed during this time period, when questions arose about this fighting, that it had been caused by an ABiH attack, an attack on the 16th of April on the HVO headquarters in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was mentioned that the reason why the HVO was taken, the BiH -- was because of a BiH attack on the HVO headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Fine. Did you have occasion, in fact, sir, to be at the HVO headquarters in Vitez several days after the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was there around the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you see any evidence of an attack on the Vitez headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir -- was it the ECMM assessment that this story of an attack on the HVO headquarters was essentially only used as an excuse or cover for the HVO attacks on the Muslim villages in the Lasva Valley?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the 17th of April 1993. Is it correct, sir, that on your way from Zenica to Vitez, not only yourself but with two other ECMM monitors, you passed the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: At the junction of the main road and the road into Ahmici you saw three bodies, possibly a family, in civilian clothes laid side by side in front of a house?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, sir, that this was a father, mother, and approximately ten year old boy?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can direct the usher, please, to show you Exhibit 1598.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that this was a photograph taken by your colleague, Erik Friis-Pederson?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And that's what you saw and you just described to us in your testimony just now?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that as you travelled in the Vitez area during the 16th and 17th of April 1993 and thereabouts, did it appear to you that the HVO had essentially sealed off the entire Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, there were a lot of checkpoints around in that area, HVO checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that around this time you learned from BritBat that the HVO was trying to ethnically cleanse some Muslim houses near the BritBat camp?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You actually saw this occur, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I saw the BritBat sitting there, in position to protect the civilians around the BritBat camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to determine that because of the intervention by the British forces, this moving of the Muslims out of their houses was prevented?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that what you and other ECMM members saw in connection with the HVO attacks on Muslim villages followed a certain system or pattern?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There appeared to be a regular pattern of, first, there would be an attack by mortars or rockets, then the village and area would be sealed off by the HVO soldiers, and then HVO squads, often wearing black balaclavas, would then attack the individual Muslim houses and murder Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When I say that was the pattern, is that the report that you heard over and over again from one village to the next?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that was the reports I heard, and some of the teams observed these soldiers at checkpoints, soldiers with ski masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the 19th of April 1993. Were you in Zenica on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And around 9.30 in the morning did you hear artillery shells being fired into the centre of Zenica town?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct that you then went to that location where the shells had landed, together with your colleague, Lars Baggesen?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You were able to determine that six shells had been fired into the Zenica marketplace killing 13 Muslim civilians and wounding many others?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I want to direct your attention, with the usher's assistance, please, to three photographs marked collectively as Exhibit 2281. Looking at the first of that package of three, is that a photograph of a shell crater, or an impact in Zenica that you -- and you took this photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The second photograph is of a destroyed car. Is that a vehicle -- excuse me. Is that a photograph you took in connection with the Zenica shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Going to the third paragraph -- excuse me -- photograph. Is that a picture that was taken by Mr. Baggesen in connection with the Zenica shelling?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is that you standing toward the right side of the photograph?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And there is another shell impact, is it correct, approximately a little less than 9.00 from your position in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If the usher -- I am going to move through these very quickly. It's probably not even necessary that they all be put on the ELMO. But if the witness could be shown Exhibits 2277,1, point 2, point 3 and point 4, and also 2282,1. We are over halfway through the outline, Your Honours. Looking at those photographs, are those additional photographs in connection with the Zenica shelling that you saw, that Mr. Baggesen took that day or others, and do they accurately show what you saw, at least in part, on that day?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There are several photographs, just for the record, of a destroyed car. There is another crater of a kiosk and a car. There is photographs showing some of the bodies of the casualties; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There is an impact near a cafe with chairs outside; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, let me ask you: As of the 19th of April 1993, the day this shelling took place, had you been serving up to that point continuously since 1983 with the Danish artillery forces?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During that time were you the operations officer?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I was operations officer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: During that time were you the commander of an artillery battery?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you in that regard received various training in the use of artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Firing of artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you received training in various artillery munitions?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Had you been trained concerning the effects or characteristics of artillery in terms of its impact in the field?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, this was -- essentially, you are, if you will, a part-time citizen soldier?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What in some countries might be called the National Guard?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You continued, in fact, to be in that capacity now?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I am still doing it now, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you now still the commander of an artillery battery?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you looked at the scene in Zenica on 19th of April 1993, is it correct, sir, that you concluded that these shells had been fired from a 122 millimetre artillery piece, having an approximate range -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I believe that this matter is contested and that the examination should take place in the conventional way, if it's acceptable to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Laustsen, can you inform the Court of your conclusions about the type of artillery that was used to fire these shells into Zenica on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. We collected some of the shrapnel that we could find in that area and took it to -- I can't remember if it was the Canadian Battalion or the British Battalion, and looked at the shrapnels and decided that it was from a 122 millimetre gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Generally speaking, can you tell the Court what the approximate range of a 122 millimetre gun is?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Approximately around 14 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was this just your own personal assessment or did the BritBat or CanBat officers, whichever it was, did they reach the same conclusion?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was a conclusion we reached together.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, can you tell the Court what steps you then took to assess, if you will, to determine the direction from which the shelling had come?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. When the shell hits the ground, it hits in a special way. Because of the speed of the shell, the fragment will be thrown out in different directions. And can we look at one of the photos again?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. Which one would you like? The first of your packet?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was this one. 2281.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes. If you can show us that, please.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. It's easy to see here. Impact place is [Indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: And you can see the shrapnel has hit the earth around here [Indicating]. When the shrapnel is situate around there, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It indicates that the shell is from this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From the direction of the pointer?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In that direction?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And the impact effects, if you will, the shrapnel effects that you see on the crater, or on the impact spot, are those sometimes referred to as splash marks?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And from that, among other things, that is how, not only you, but other military people assess the direction from which a shell was fired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That's a commonly accepted method of doing so; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you also take a compass reading?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. On the opposite, three or four metres away from the crater, and just used a compass in the normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: What reading did you -- do you recall which reading --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was around 270.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would that put it in roughly a westerly direction from --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was straight west, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you and Mr. Baggesen and the BritBat or CanBat officers then able to come to some conclusion as to an approximate location where the shells had been fired?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was around the Travnik area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Did you know at that time who -- what forces on the ground controlled that particular territory?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Usher, you just sat down, but if I could have your assistance again, please. If the witness could be shown -- perhaps he has them up there -- if the witness could be shown Exhibit 2282,6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at Exhibit 2282,6, in which a bearing has been drawn on this topographic grid of the Zenica area, is that a fair representation, sir, of the approximate location which you and Mr. Baggesen and the BritBat or CanBat officers determined that the firing had come from?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you able to determine, in the course of your ECMM duties on the 19th of April, whether there were, in fact, any military targets near the marketplace in Zenica which could reasonably have been the aiming point for these artillery shells?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: As far as I knew or know, there were -- there wasn't any military objects around the marketplace.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Could you look, please, at -- if the usher could show you Exhibit 2282,4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you could hand him 2282,5 at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Looking at the map of -- this is a map of Zenica, for the record -- and looking at the location marked in blue as an "M" with a circle, do you agree, sir, that that's the approximate location of the marketplace in Zenica where the shells impacted?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention also to the accompanying exhibit, 2282,5, do you see, please, that that is a legend or key to the map, to the circled location on the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And for the record, Your Honours, and to be clear, there are other numbers on this map for different reasons, but the numbers to which the key responds are those in bold circled print, the closest one to the "M" being at approximately 8.00 position, number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, as an artillery officer, as the commander of an artillery battery, were there any military targets within a reasonable margin of error from the impact points in the Zenica marketplace?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it your assessment that this artillery fire, then, was intentionally directed at a civilian target?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, just a moment. I think that's a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Rephrase it in a neutral way, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps the best way, again, is to just simply ask you: Based on your familiarity with Zenica during your time in Bosnia, and assisted by the map which is Exhibit 2282,4, were there any military targets within a reasonable range, if you will, or close by the location where the shells impacted on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving ahead, is it correct, sir, that during your time in Central Bosnia, the HVO controlled the PTT or telephone lines in the area and communicated effectively between the various HVO components and locations, including Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that in working with Mr. Baggesen and others, that it appeared to you that -- it appeared to be the case that the PTT lines were mostly functional or could easily have been repaired?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was it ECMM's conclusion in most of these instances that in fact all the HVO really needed to do was switch on the lines?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That was our conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention further, you were in Kiseljak on a number of occasions during your tour of duty; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You did not meet the HVO commander there, Ivica Rajic?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: However, you did speak with Mario Bradara, the deputy HVO commander; Vinko Lukic, who was one of the HVO brigade commanders; and Vinko Frankovic, who was the HVO information officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, moving to the 27th of April, 1993, is it correct, sir, that you and other monitors attempted on the 27th of April to enter several Muslim villages near Kiseljak, including Gomionica, but the HVO stopped you from entering the villages?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you told by the HVO officer on site that the HVO commander in that region, Ivica Rajic, had ordered, in fact, that all U.N., UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and ECMM vehicles be stopped and prevented from entering those villages?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to show you Exhibit 836,1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is a daily summary for the 27th of April, 1993, for RC Zenica. Directing your attention to the second page, sir, are you one of the persons who -- I guess I can't say signed, but whose name is listed under the document -- under the text?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention specifically to paragraph 2, immediately above your name, if you could just look at that for a moment, is that an accurate account of your efforts to enter the village Gomionica on the 27th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And in fact you record there this order by commander Ivica Rajic to stop all U.N.-related vehicles; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward to the 29th of April, did you and Mr. Baggesen and others, with the assistance of an armed escort by CanBat, the Canadian Battalion, you actually then succeeded in visiting the villages of Polje Visnjica, Hercezi, Doci, Visnjica, and Gomionica, again, all of which were located in the Kiseljak area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was the reason that you had gone to these villages, first on the 27th and again on the 29th, was because of reports that those Muslim villages had been ethnically cleansed by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that you found in Polje Visnjica that the only, in fact, few houses which had not been burned or destroyed were the houses where Bosnian Croats lived?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But that all the Muslim houses had been destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that the Muslim families in Hercezi had good relations with their Bosnian Croat neighbours, and that was probably why the Muslim houses in that village had not been burned?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: But, in fact, nonetheless, approximately 14 Muslim civilians had been killed in that area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You found that the village of Doci was completely abandoned?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In Visnjica, approximately 40 out of 115 Muslim houses had been destroyed by the HVO, and five Muslim men had been killed?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And about -- when you arrived there on the 29th, your team was able to determine that approximately 20 Muslim families had returned to the village at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is it correct, sir, that none of the Muslim civilians in the above villages that we've just talked about were allowed to pass out of the HVO checkpoint at Polje Visnjica?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And finally, was it your conclusion or -- excuse me, observation that the Muslim village of Gomionica was destroyed and completely abandoned?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If I can ask you to look briefly at Exhibit 847, is that a copy of a report that you and Mr. Baggesen prepared concerning the inspection of these villages on the 29th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You agree today, still, with the conclusions stated in paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Moving forward, if the usher could show you, if he has it with him already, we can just finish up with 902,1, 915, 921, and 1041. I want to direct your attention, sir, please, to the 11th of May, 1993. Is it correct that around that date you had a meeting in Fojnica --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- with the local BiH commander, Beba Nasuf, and the local HVO commander, Stjepan Tuka?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you find that the general situation in Fojnica was calm and without tension, as the Muslims and Croats were living together peacefully?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did both Mr. Nasuf and Mr. Tuka report that they had good relations with each other, they had daily meetings and joint patrols, and the only issue that they were dealing with at that particular time was that Mr. Tuka, commander Tuka, was having problems with his HVO superiors because of his good dealings with the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you look, please, at Exhibit 902,1. Is that your report from the 11th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And basically it recounts what we've just -- your testimony just now; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, on the 12th or 13th of May, is it correct that you also talked with the mayor of Fojnica?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Nasir Salimovic?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: He told you that by that day, which we're now a day or two later, Mr. Tuka had been dismissed as the HVO commander in the area because he had too good relations with the Muslims and would not follow an order to attack?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. This matter is contested. It's double hearsay, and I believe Mr. Tuka is on the Prosecutor's witness list, so he can talk about this for himself. In fact, he was actually listed as being one of the witnesses for this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, this witness can say what he heard. Of course, if Mr. Tuka gives evidence, that will be the most direct evidence of what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The only problem that I have with what he heard, Your Honour, is that he is actually reporting what someone else had heard from someone else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that you have a problem, but we're admitting it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you can look, please, we can move very quickly, look at Exhibit 915. Is that your report from the 13th of May?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to Item 7, does it reference your conversation with the mayor? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And even at that time, as stated here, the Croats and Muslims in Fojnica were not having yet any problems; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, looking at Exhibit 921 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, it's past 1.00. Are you going to be many more minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Literally probably two or three minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you look at Exhibit 921, is that your report from the 14th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just for identification purposes, on the lower right portion of the page, the writing "22nd August" and then followed by a signature, is that yours?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's mine, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Directing your attention to approximately the middle of the page, the end of Item Number 2, were you informed that day that, quote, "The HVO commander has been removed from his job because too good relationships with the BiH. However, the commander is still on his job"?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Were you surprised to learn, only a short time after the 14th of May and after Mr. Tuka had been removed, that, in fact, fighting did break out between the HVO and ABiH in the Fojnica area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was surprised at all that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Last exhibit, last question, if you look at Exhibit 1041, the second page, which is an RC Zenica report for the 10th of June, 1993, directing your attention to the bottom part of the page -- the last paragraph on page 2, sorry. In connection with your testimony, sir, did you learn -- did ECMM learn, at least by the 10th of June, that, in fact, the BiH commander in Fojnica informed the team that the HVO some days ago ordered the Croats who live in the Muslim part of the town to move into the Croat part of the town; the Croats are now moving back?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: That was after Mr. Tuka had been removed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll adjourn now. Mr. Laustsen, would you please remember not to speak to anybody during the adjournment about your evidence, and that includes members of the Prosecution team. Would you be back, please, at 2.35.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.05 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Laustsen. My name is Steven Sayers and I am representing one of the attorneys representing Dario Kordic. You were in Bosnia-Herzegovina from April the 1st to June the 30th, 1993, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you took a holiday, I believe of 11 days, from May the 20th to June the 1st out of the country?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which meant that you spent a grand total of about ten weeks in the country, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What did you do, before you arrived in Bosnia on April the 1st, to read up or study up on the political, military or historical situation in the country?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Actually, in Denmark I was following the situation in the newspapers, in television. And I started -- when I volunteered -- what's it called -- a course, where I learned about the situation in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How long did that course last?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I think it was two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Two days?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Two days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You've lived in Denmark, I take it, all of your life?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And you've been in -- a policeman for the last 15 years?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Since '84. Yes, 15 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. As I understand it, you received a standard ECMM briefing?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were informed that the military commander of the HVO in Central Bosnia operative zone was who?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the Muslim military forces commander was whom?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Hadzihasanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: General Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who was the ECMM telling you, if they did, was the political leader of the Muslims in Central Bosnia, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember. I was told, but I can't remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As a general matter, Mr. Laustsen, as unfortunate and tragic as the fact may be, burned out houses were a common sight in Bosnia in both Croat and Muslim villages when you were there; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, the same is true of the Croat sections in Muslim villages, predominantly Muslim villages, and of the Muslim sections in predominantly Croat villages, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, once again, as unfortunate and tragic it may be, but nonetheless a fact of the area, one of the routine techniques used by both sides in this war was to burn down the houses of enemy civilians once a village had been taken, if you like. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of your colleagues, Major Baggesen, described this as sort of a cycle of retribution and revenge. Would that be in accordance with the way that you saw things?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Indeed, your colleague, Major Baggesen, maintained a war diary, which is already in evidence in this case, and he observed that he had travelled around on April the 20th, and I believe it may have been with you, visiting some Croatian villages that had been burned down, and making the observation that many houses had been abandoned, criminal gangs ran riot and pillaged houses. That's on page 8 of his diary. Did you see that too?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: His diary? Yes. Sometime I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The facts that are recorded in his diary, you were witness to those facts as well, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Some of them. Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And when these terrible things happened in the ECMM, of which you as one of the monitors got involved, it was equally routine for both sides, basically, to point the finger at the other? Wouldn't that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You mentioned, and I am going to try to go through this extremely briefly, because I want to get you out of here by the end of the day, if possible, sir. You referred to a truck convoy, I think it consisted of four trucks that had been hijacked in the town of Vitez or Vitez on April the 12th. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That convoy or those trucks were actually carrying foodstuffs, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On April the 8th or thereabouts there was an incident that caused some tension when a HZHB flag was raised outside of the headquarters of the 7th Muslim brigade in Travnik. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it true that on the same day there was a huge military parade in Travnik with about 1.000 soldiers from the 17th Krajina brigade, the 7th Muslim Brigade, and various other so-called ABiH detachments?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. That's fair enough. Let me just read you, for the purposes of saving time, an extract from Exhibit Z693, which is an ECMM monitor mission Danish delegation communication to Zagreb. In the Travnik area, and I am reading from page 10 now, it says: "A parade took place at the old JNA barracks to commemorate the first anniversary of the BiH Army. About 1.000 soldiers paraded with elements from the 306th, 312th, 17th Krajina and 7th Muslim brigades." Does that jog your memory about that particular incident, or have you still -- I mean, I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. Do you recall an incident a few days after that where four HVO staff officers were kidnapped just outside the town of Novi Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You were returning from the front line with the Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was to the north and west, I think?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So the HVO actually had units fighting the Serbs up in that area to the northwest of Novi Travnik, and to the west of Travnik, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Croats at the front line, yes

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And these four unfortunate fellows were kidnapped by the 7th Muslim Brigade, were they not?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: At what -- August.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. And it ultimately turned out to be true; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Their release was from some Mujahedins.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Right. In terms of the release that you've just talked about, were you actually present when the prisoners were released in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I was watching from my window in the hotel. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That was a pretty lively occasion, I think, would be an understated way to put it; wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, I believe -- and this is Exhibit D79/1 I'll just read from -- it's an ECMM document a special report, dated May the 19th, 1993. Let me just ask you to tell me whether this is consistent with the event that you've describe. "At Zenica, in front of the Hotel International, the Mujahedin showed up with a force of at least 100 masked and heavily armed soldiers, probably members of the 7th Muslim Brigade." Please, forgive me for pausing, but I'm a notorious victim of the interpreters, and I need to make sure that they can keep up. The comment goes on to say: "They deployed a three-barrel 20-milimetre machine gun mounted on a five-ton truck, anti-tank and anti-aircraft shoulder-launched missiles. The situation here was explosive. All local and military police forces disappeared from the scene when the Mujahedin arrived. When the released Arabians arrived and got out of the UNPROFOR armed carriers, they were cheered by a crowd of some 100 people, and after that they were escorted from the spot by the masked soldiers who fired their weapons into the air when leaving." Is that pretty much what you saw?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I saw, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Immediately before the fighting broke out, Mr. Laustsen, on the 16th of April or before then, you were one of the people that actually went to the scene of the Totic kidnapping; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see the four unfortunate bodyguards who had been executed in the car?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I saw four dead bodies in the car, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: There was also a civilian who was --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: A civilian, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware that forces stationed in Kruscica and Stari Vitez had threatened retaliatory action against the HVO on the night of April the 15th unless two abducted or detained ABiH soldiers were released?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just show you two documents and see if that jogs your memory. The first is the 1st battalion of the Cheshire Regiment, milinfosum number 167, dated April the 15th, 1993. I might ask the usher to show you this. The second document is a product from the G2 milinfosum of the headquarters command in Kiseljak of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The first document is marked D93/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Unfortunately we don't actually have copies of the second document with us, but if I might ask the usher to place my copy on the ELMO, I can just point out the part that I would like to bring to your attention. I won't burden the record with reading out what the document says; we'll have this marked as an exhibit in due course. But you can see there that actually BiH sources revealed to BritBat that they had, in fact, launched an attack on Vitez at about 5.30 a.m. on the 16th of April; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, the British battalion recorded the fact that threats had been made regarding the abduction of the two ABiH soldiers, and those threats came from the commander of the 325th Brigade in Vitez; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Good. And if you would just take a look at the document that we have just marked, the British milinfosum, on page 1 and 2, if you just show that to the witness, Mr. Usher. It's about halfway down the second full paragraph. I'd just like to read into the record that "Sefkija Dzidic stated that if the HVO did not release the two BiH soldiers and return the weapons soon, he would not be able to account for the actions of his soldiers." And that was followed up by a statement made by a gentleman who is identified here as Ramiz Dugavic, but I think his name is Ramiz Dugalic, who was the commander of the 325th Brigade, that the situation would deteriorate rapidly if the release of the two BiH soldiers did not occur immediately. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And if you just take a look over at the top of the next page on this, the British intelligence cell concludes that if the two BiH soldiers are not returned soon, some form of retaliatory action by the BiH against the HVO is highly likely. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. And just to conclude this line of questioning, Mr. Laustsen, my understanding is that you did not actually visit Vitez until the 20th; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Which was four days after the fighting broke out?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Turning to the Zenica shelling incident, it's true, and I think you will agree with this, that Zenica was routinely shelled both before and after April the 19th; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It started around the 18th of April, the shelling, and continued after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In other words, the shelling of Zenica started on the afternoon and evening of the 18th, the day before the incident --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: In that area yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And thereafter, as unfortunate as it may be, Zenica was shelled relatively frequently, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, in fact, I believe on page 14 of your colleague's war diary Major Baggesen records that in the afternoon Zenica and Vitez were subjected to a fierce artillery attack. "On average we were attacked every other day." Is that consistent with your recollection? Now, you say that Zenica was shelled at about 9.30 a.m.; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It could be another time but, it was -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
