utterances.text: In your statement at page 6, the only reason I raise the subject is that you state that: "I can recollect that on the 19th of April, 1993, around noon, I heard artillery shells being fired into the centre of Zenica." And you made that statement on August the 21st and 22nd, 1996?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So was it 9.30 or was it noon?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It must be noon then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: It must be noon?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your colleague, Major Baggesen, actually recorded in his contemporaneous journal that: "Without warning an artillery attack was launched on Zenica with shells falling in the town centre and near our hotel. The attack began at 09.30 hours."

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So it was at 9.30?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was frequently, everyday. I can't say one day from another.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was Remi Landry also an ECMM monitor --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: -- present during this indent?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you say that six shells fell into the centre of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Around six shell, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me just read you a section from Mr. Landry's statement, which was taken pretty much contemporaneously with yours in August of 1996. "On the 19th of April 1993, at about 12.10 hours I was in my room in the Hotel International in Zenica. I heard two rockets land in the direction of the centre of Zenica town. Into the centre of town. Two additional rockets landed at 12.24 hours and a further two fell at 12.29 hours. I made a record in my diary of the times these rockets fell. "Thereafter, I heard two other rockets fall at 12.48 hours, which makes eight by my count, and 12.58 hours. Further away from the town at 13.16 hours and 13.43 hours two fell to the south, which makes 10, and north out of the town. At 13.56 hours and 14.04 hours two rockets were heard falling further away." Which makes 12 artillery rounds. Now, were they rockets or were they shells that were falling into the town? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Shells in the town, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Was it six or was it twelve?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Can I look in my diary for a moment? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, we have not been provided with that diary.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It's because it's not -- I haven't used it before, not under my interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness look at the diary, just to refresh his memory on that particular point.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: My diary I write: At 12.10 the city was hit by artillery fire, first two rounds, then the sirens were activated. And after that I counted four rounds within 20 minutes into the centre of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How about the other rounds that --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I haven't made any notes about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. So in your contemporaneous diary the shelling occurred at about midday?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you visited the scene of the shelling along with Major Baggesen how many minutes or hours after the incident had occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember that. I have to -- I was looking at the scene several times. A few days after there were shellings during a high level meeting in Zenica where the commanders were present. They were making a ceasefire agreement. And during that meeting the town was shelled again. Then I was investigating together with soldiers from, I think it was ABiH and HVO. So it's -- I have more times that the points --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: But the question was: How soon after the shelling incident did you actually visit the scene of the incident to do your investigation, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, you, I take it, collected various pieces of shrapnel from the shells, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you actually find any fuses?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What kind of fuse does a 152-millimetre shell actually have, at the time that you were in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It would mean that it's the fuse that is actuated when it hit the ground. I don't know the name in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You don't recall the actual designation? All right. Did you know, actually, that the fuses and the majority of the fragments had actually been collected up by an investigating judge from Zenica, who proceeded to conduct his own investigation?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, sir: Isn't it true that for a 152 or 155-caliber shell, the fuse with a designation 0F462Z is used. Is that a designation that's familiar to you at all?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So if you actually saw an OF462Z shell, you really wouldn't know what calibre of shell it came from, would you?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't know it, no. That's why I have some expert from the CanBat or the BritBat to help.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to the investigating judge who performed this investigation, Mr. Mladen Veseljak?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I didn't know there was an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you know that it was his conclusion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know that there was an investigation. So that's as far as you can take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Isn't it possible, sir, in your expert opinion, that the shell could actually have been a 155-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Millimetre. You can't exclude that possibility, can you, based upon the little fragments of what was remaining of the shell --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: But it wasn't my conclusion alone. It was somebody at CanBat that was used to looking at fragments and to see what kind of ammunition it was. I can't say "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the range of a 152-millimetre M84 artillery piece is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I guess it's around 15 or 17 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me put it to you that the 152-millimetre howitzer, model M84, has a range of 24,4 kilometres, extended. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Howitzer? 152?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: 24,4 kilometres. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No. I know that in Denmark we, at that time, had some 155 millimetres. They were shooting around 15 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: On the subject of a 155 millimetre piece of ordnance, sir, an M46/84 model actually has an extended range of 39,6 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, a new model, yes, with a new ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you see any 155-millimetre howitzers anywhere when you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Where are the fragments that you collected up on the 19th of April 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: They were delivered at the CanBat or the BritBat. I still can't remember which of the places it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make a record of the number or shape of these particular fragments?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make any record of them being delivered to whoever it was that you delivered them to?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Would you agree that it is at least possible, in your opinion, within a regional margin of error, that the direction of fire actually could have come from the extreme southwest, and not 270 degrees due west, as you testified?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: In the place I investigated, I would say from 265 to 275, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: A 10 degree margin of error, plus or minus?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Five.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. How many minutes was it between rounds, as far as you remember, between the six rounds that you heard?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I have written 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. With the Trial Chamber's permission, let me just read you from the testimony that Mr. Veseljak gave in the Blaskic case on the 22nd of January, 1998. Page 5949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: He is the investigating judge, Your Honour, who came up with conclusions regarding the source of the fire and the direction and the interval between rounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you could put the conclusions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me put it to you, sir, maybe you'll agree with him, maybe you'll disagree. His conclusion was that the direction of fire came from the extreme southwest. You could not exclude that possibility, could you?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Extreme --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Extreme southwest?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: What would you mean with extreme?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, I would say 180 degrees to --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You would exclude that. All right. And Mr. Veseljak concludes that there was less than a minute between shells. Is that consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: They were the two first shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you actually participate with the local police forces or investigate in any way regarding the source of the shells that fell onto Zenica on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you prepare any written reports, sir?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I'm sure that there was a written report, yes. I'm not sure which of the -- as I told you before, I looked at several shells several days, two days later, I think, during that -- this meeting. I was doing some investigation again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, are you telling the Court that there was a written report prepared by you and your colleagues, or do you recall one not being prepared at all?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I prepared one, but if it was the first or the second, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to it?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I delivered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: To whom?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: To the RC Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me just cover some potential variables with you. Would you agree with me that the longer the range that you are shooting over, the lesser of the accuracy you can predict?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And, indeed, the accuracy of the particular artillery piece depends to some extent upon a tube life; in other words, the number of rounds that have actually been shot through the barrel, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: The more rounds that are shot through a barrel, the less predictable the fall of shot becomes?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And a howitzer is different from other ordnance, in that it generally flies at a higher trajectory than regular cannons or large calibre weapons, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the apogee of the ballistic trajectory of 122 or 152 or 155 millimetre shells is?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The apogee?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Apogee of the ballistic trajectory, the high point on the trajectory.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That depends on the range.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. At maximum range you've testified, in your view, maximum range of a 122-millimetre weapon is 14 to 15 kilometres, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: What is the high point on the ballistic trajectory at maximum range, sir? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One of the variables, meteorologically anyway, that governs the accuracy of fall of shot is actually the wind conditions at the various elevations that you can predict a shell passing through?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the meteorological conditions on the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know whether the HVO had any forward observers to observe the fall of shot and correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you know what the angle of impact of the shell actually was?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No, I can't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you perform any calculations regarding the angle of impact?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Given the fact that howitzers generally fire at larger trajectories, isn't it true that the shorter the range, the higher the trajectory, and therefore the more -- the greater the angle of impact --

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The shorter -- the higher?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You wouldn't agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: How do you aim a weapon at a shorter range? Do you use a lesser charge?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what kind of a charge was used on any of the shots that were fired on the 19th?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you say that your ECMM monitors or your fellow monitors, you were the most knowledgeable about things regarding -- involving artillery?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't think so. Maybe. As always, there are more clever persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Absolutely. But do you know of anybody who was an artillery commander who was an ECMM monitor at the time that you were?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I think later on there came a German, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you make a recommendation for the installation of artillery locating radar in the Zenica area, to eliminate any doubts as to where shots may have come from and who was firing at whom?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: We were talking about it, yes, and we were told that the two that were in Sarajevo, they were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, you have been shown, and it's been introduced as Exhibit Z836,1, a daily summary from the regional centre in Zenica, which says: "The joint operation command had a meeting today with the mayor of Vitez. They discussed the hum problems in the area." "Hum" was actually a high feature which was an artillery location; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And the summary goes on to say that: "The ECMM monitors strongly feel that this situation could be resolved once and for all if locating battery could be made available to clarify this situation once and for all." And in the actual daily operational report for the same day, the observation was made that: "The problem to verify firing units and targets must be solved so that there is no question of who is firing on who. The only way to do that is by artillery locating radar."

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In your professional opinion, would you say that that's accurate?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, because it can tell you where the shelling are coming from. The investigation on the spot can only tell you in what direction the firing was coming from, not the exact place of the gun, howitzer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, do you remember, or perhaps you don't remember this, that there was another incident involving shelling on May the 8th of 1993, and feel free to consult your diary, where Zenica and Vitez were shelled, and an investigation was done by the ECMM that resulted in the production of a written report? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: [No audible response].

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I could ask the usher to show you the exhibit that was marked as D90/1. We have put on the ELMO, Mr. Laustsen, a report that was actually prepared regarding a shelling incident that was used -- that involved the use of 152-millimetre ordnance. Were you involved in this investigation at all?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You can see that the Muslims had accused the Croats of being responsible, precisely reciprocal accusations were made, and the monitor or monitors that prepared this report stated that it was a relief to tell both sides that Serbs had fired at both these towns?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, it would be fair to conclude, would it not, that there's absolutely no question that both Vitez and Zenica were well within range of Serb artillery at this time?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And before?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a few questions regarding the Kiseljak fighting that you touched upon. The village of Hercezi, where no houses were burned, was located well to the west of the main supply route that connected or ran from Busovaca through Kacuni and Bilalovac to Kiseljak; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It's hard for me to remember the exact places.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: That's fair enough. While we are locating a map on that, let me just ask you to agree, and feel free to disagree if it's inaccurate. All of the villages where you saw the damage in the Kiseljak valley, they all were located right next to or on the high ground overlooking the main road?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I was going to ask you some questions in connection with ceasefire agreements, but maybe I do not need to. You will agree that you never met Mr. Kordic, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Never spoke to him, right?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Then I'll move on. Let me turn for a brief instant to the Muslim forces offensive that occurred in the second week of June of 1993, sir. There is no question that a large offensive was launched by ABiH forces on Travnik between June the 8th and 12th, is there?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that offensive involved lots of casualties and thousands of refugees. I can't give you a precise number, but I can tell you that the estimates range from 5.000 to about 20.000 refugees. Is that consistent with what you were hearing at the time?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not as I remember. Not that many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. How many were -- how many refugees resulted from that offensive, as best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't give you a figure, because I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Fair enough. Pretty much simultaneously between June the 9th and June the 13th, a similar offensive was taking place in the Kakanj area; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I think it is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And that actually did result in a huge efflux of refugees, numbering around 15.000. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I remember a lot of refugees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the Fojnica fighting about which you gave some testimony, that actually occurred just a few days after you had left the region; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I know they were fighting when I went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Actually, the fighting broke out on July the 2nd, just about two days after General Morillon had visited the city and applauded it as being an oasis of peace and a safe haven; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. But fighting did break out around July the 2nd?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The start of July -- June.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: July the 2nd, I believe, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I wasn't down there July the 2nd, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware of what the result of that fighting was?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you left Central Bosnia, would it be fair to say that there were just a few isolated Croat enclaves, one from Busovaca to Vitez, the Kiseljak enclave, the Kakanj enclave had actually been eliminated, there was an enclave in Zepce too. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And all of these enclaves were geographically isolated from one another and surrounded by ABiH forces, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The Kiseljak area was -- I don't think they were, but some of them were isolated, yes, and surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let's take Kiseljak then. It was surrounded on three sides by Muslims and on the other side by Serbs, wasn't it, right?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I think that's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Were you present in Kiseljak on June the 22nd when a rocket attack killed several children in the Croat part of the town and wounded several other people?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Let me turn to Zepce for just a minute. You visited the Zepce area, I believe, on May the 4th?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I have been in the Zepce area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You prepared a report, I'm happy to show you a copy of it, but maybe it's not necessary. Do you remember meeting a gentleman, the head of the HVO government in Zepce, a gentleman by the name of Perica Jukic?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You spoke with him? He was also a member of the HDZ party or the HDZ BiH, right?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you ever follow this gentleman's career at all after you visited him on May the 4th of 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't think so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So you don't have any knowledge of the prominent political positions which he ultimately assumed?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. You gave some testimony regarding a gentleman by the name of Stjepan Tuka, and this was the last area of testimony that I have for you. You say that Mr. Tuka was removed. Did you actually speak to him?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not after it had been told, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did you speak to him before he was removed?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Did he tell you that he had actually disobeyed two combat orders?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: He told me that -- I don't know if it was two, but he told me that he had to attack the BiH when he was ordered to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Who gave those orders to him?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Supposedly, his superior officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Wouldn't you agree with me that it's not unusual for a military commander who disobeys combat orders to be removed from office?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It's not unusual.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: In fact, it's absolutely normal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Now, the orders that Mr. Tuka was given didn't require him to attack civilians and eliminate them, did they?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I don't know his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: All right. Did you know that the gentleman to whom you spoke, the Muslim military commander, was also removed pretty much at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: As Mr. Tuka?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And did you know that the Croats were basically pushed out of Fojnica at the end of June and July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I know they were -- yes, sometime, but as I remember, they were moving back before I left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: So we have Mr. Tuka removed and the commanders that he was cooperating with removed as well, and replaced by new commanders who fell to fighting within --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think the witness can answer all of this. That's all a matter of comment. Anything else for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Any questions, Mr. Kovacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I will be very brief in my questions. Good afternoon, Mr. Laustsen, my name is Goran Mikulicic and together with Mr. Kovacic representing Mr. Cerkez in these proceedings. Mr. Laustsen, you said that on 12 April 1993 a convoy consisting of four trucks which transported foodstuffs was abducted. Can you give us the exact location where this took place?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It's difficult for me because I wasn't involved in this personally in that matter. I just remember it happened. So I can't give you an exact location, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you say approximately in the territory of what municipality did this took place?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the -- it was in the Vitez area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that the regional centre at Zenica received information on 16 April that the ABiH army had attacked the main HVO headquarters in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you visit this location?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The HQ of the HVO army, only a few days later. I think it was around the 20th of April I was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember in what building the headquarters was set up?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Would you recognise the building if I showed you a photograph of it?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was going through the place in an APC and was in the APC until we stopped in front of the building and I looked at the building. We had to have a talk with, as far as I remember, with Blaskic, because of some roadblocks. That's the reason we were there, so I'm not sure I can --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, would your memory be refreshed if I told you that this was the building of a local hotel?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we will not pursue this line of questioning. At one point you said during your examination-in-chief that the HVO controlled the PTT lines. We agreed that in the Lasva Valley there were several enclaves under the HVO control and which were surrounded by the ABiH forces. In this context, that is the way the forces were deployed, would it be correct for me to infer that I can interpret your statement to have meant that the HVO had control over those PTT lines which were lying in the area under its control?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: One of the PTT, I think it was in Kiseljak, that it was only a matter of an order. Then it was able to talk on the telephone in most of the area from Kiseljak to Travnik, Zenica. It was only a matter of switching it on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that the ABiH army -- the ABiH did control other PTT lines in the territory under its control?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That's possible. I can't answer you "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, during the examination-in-chief you were shown the daily operational report for 24 July 1993, and in order to save time I am just going to refer you to the excerpts that I am interested in. In point 1(a) of this report, that is -- sorry, the 26th of April, an area in the vicinity of the British Battalion came under an artillery attack. Do you know the location where the British Battalion had its base?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes. I was staying there a lot of time. It was -- ECMM had a house just next to the British Battalion. I don't know the address, if that's ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of course. Then you certainly know what military units controlled this area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: The area around the BritBat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What units were those? Were those the HVO or the ABiH units?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: It was the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, my understanding is that you did not spend much time in Vitez. Do you know the organisation of the HVO military in the Vitez area?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not as I can tell you how it was. I was attending some meetings in the ECMM house in Vitez with this joint command, it was called at the time, but I can't remember the names of the people who were -- participated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I were to put to you the name of Mario Cerkez, would you remember it as someone with whom you ever spoke?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can't remember it, no

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This concludes my cross-examination, Your Honours. Thank you, Mr. Laustsen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. If the usher could show the witness, please, 2282,6, 2282,4 and 2281, the photograph of the -- one of the impacts. If you can just put that in front of him. Mr. Laustsen, I am going to ask you first to look at the large map, the topographical map, please, which is 2282,6. Zenica, the Court may or may not know at this point or appreciate, that Zenica is a fairly large town. Is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: By Bosnian standards. And looking at Exhibit 2286. If I can use the term, the greater Zenica area extends along the river, stems out to the east of the city along the road to the -- excuse me, to the west and the east, for that matter. So you see the area, the larger Zenica area? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, when Mr. Sayers asked you: Had Zenica been shelled prior to the 19th of April 1993, do you know what parts of Zenica had been shelled, what areas, what locations the Zenica area had been shelled prior to the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you have any information that any place near the civilian marketplace had ever been shelled prior to the 19th of April?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: There was testimony about 122 millimetre, 155 millimetre and 152 millimetre. Some of those numbers are quite similar. Was it your conclusion, sir, that these shells that struck Zenica on the 19th of April were 122 millimetre?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: My conclusion, together with them from the BritBat or the CanBat, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And in your experience, is that quite different than a 155-millimetre shell?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, concerning the names. You said at one point you didn't know the name of a particular fuse or a designation of some numbers that Mr. Sayers referred you to. Is it correct to say, and I think you said this. Your Honour, I think the witness said this, but it didn't come through on the transcript. You didn't recognise those designations in English, sir? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't know their names in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In reference to Exhibit 836,1, the report from the 27th of April. Mr. Sayers referred you to a section which says: "The JOC at a meeting today with the mayor of Vitez, they discussed the hum problems in the area." Do you recall, sir, whether it was often the case that ECMM abbreviated humanitarian as "hum"?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, humanitarian officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If someone referred to a humanitarian officer or to a humanitarian issue, they might write "hum"?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Finally, looking at the photograph that's marked of the shell impact, 2281. Could you just once again on the ELMO show -- put your pointer on where you would -- where you would deduct the line of fire from that impact?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: That impact, it's right here [Indicating]. Coming this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: I can see it here [Indicating].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In terms of the so-called splash marks of the shrapnel, you would not expect to see splash marks behind from the direction from which the fire came, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Only a very, very few, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Because when the shell impacts, it basically splashes forward?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes, because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And to the side?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps, just for the record purposes, if you have a highlighter, a marker there, you could mark Exhibit 2281 with the approximate line of fire. I'm sorry, does it not -- excuse me, don't do that. Would you like him not to do that, Madam Registrar? We can get a clear version, if we need to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you got a --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: On the second version that you've just been handed, sir, could you just mark the line of fire, if you will, on that drawing?

utterances.speaker: ALLAN LAUSTSEN
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour. I would like a moment, when the witness is released, if we could have a moment of the Court's time, once the witness is released, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Laustsen, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That last exhibit had better be given an A number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The last exhibit will be number 2281/1.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Court will recall some days ago the Court requested or indicated it would be helpful to have copies of the Vance-Owen Plan and also some demographic material. I've prepared that. I have provided it to the Defence, and I placed it on the registry's desk. If that could be distributed to the three judges, I would give a momentary explanation for it. Your Honours, Exhibit 571 and 571,1 are similar but not identical documents concerning the Vance-Owen Plan. Sometimes the format presentation is different, some of the attachments were somewhat different. So I've frankly simply provided the Court with both copies. The document, the agreements themselves are identical. It's just that some of the attachments and maps might be more helpful to the Court in one version than the other. I note, just by point of reference, on 571,1 which the title page is "Security Counsel Official Records". If the Court will look to the back, the next last page of that packet, for instance, you will see a map of the Vance-Owen Plan. And this map having been signed, in fact, by a number of the parties, including Mr. Boban, Mr. Izetbegovic, Lord Owen and Cyrus Vance, this will show a map of the proposed cantons. And, of course, the one we talked about most frequently about in this case is 9, 10 and 8 with Vitez and Busovaca being in province 10. Finally, Your Honour, Exhibit 571,2 is a several page document of demographic information, as the Court requested. The first page -- all this information basically comes from the 1991 census, which I don't think there is any dispute. The only authoritative census, if you will, in Bosnia-Herzegovina shortly before the war. It lists the most pertinent municipalities to the case in alphabetical order and gives a total population and the ethnic breakdown. As one of the footnotes indicates, if the Court takes the time at some point to add up the three columns, Muslim, Croat and Serb, you will find that on some occasion it doesn't exactly equal total, because there was also some who considered themselves other or called themselves Yugoslavs. For ease of simplicity of presentation, you can certainly be provided. It's a small fraction, and in some cases don't give you quite 100 per cent. On the bottom part of the page is the percentages in terms of the proposed provinces 8, 10 and 9. There is, in the second page, Your Honour, a bar chart, which essentially presents the same percentage information by municipality. The third page, Your Honour, is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina with the outlines of what at one time was proposed as the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. And you can see by the colour codes, again based roughly on the 1991 census, the ethnic breakdown of the various municipalities. The document that follows that, the page that follows that map, Your Honour, is simply a source, an explanation, which provides details as to the source of the information for the Defence and for the Court's information. Just to have it in one attached document, the last page is again a copy of the Vance-Owen map. I think that's all we have to say, unless the Court has questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, this is very useful, 571,2. Would you be able to produce any document which shows, in the same way that this shows, the ethnic composition in 1991, something which shows the ethnic composition at the end of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We may, Your Honour. I'll inquire. I do know in general terms that because of the war and the limits on available information, I know some of these tasks have been very difficult to do. But I will inquire. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: One brief matter of detail, Mr. President. Would it be possible to have marked as the next Defence exhibit the document that I actually put on the ELMO, but due to my fault I have not had enough copies to be distributed to date. So it's the April the 17th UNPROFOR document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Make sure there is a copy for the registry, would you, so it can be probably marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I'll bring it tomorrow morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll adjourn now until Monday morning, half past 9.00.
